title: Global freedom declines continue as conflict, coups, institutional erosion, and repression narrow political and civil space
source_unit: Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2026: The Growing Shadow of Autocracy
geography: 195 countries and 13 territories assessed for calendar year 2025

denominator.unit: countries and territories assessed in Freedom in the World 2026

consecutive_global_decline.unit: consecutive years in which global freedom declined

countries_declining_2025.unit: countries with deterioration in political rights and civil liberties during 2025

countries_improving_2025.unit: countries with improvements in political rights and civil liberties during 2025

population_affected_decline.unit: more than percent of the world's population living in countries whose freedom scores declined in 2025

observations.method: Freedom House assessment of political rights and civil liberties using 25 indicators scored from 0 to 4 and aggregated into a 100-point scale.
observations.uncertainty: The assessment is an expert-coded comparative index with methodological judgments and country narratives; score changes do not measure every lived experience or establish a single cause of decline.
observations.subgroup: Countries and territories classified as Free, Partly Free, or Not Free, and populations affected by changes in political rights and civil liberties.
observations.counterinterpretation: Global decline coexists with country-level improvement, institutional resilience, and peaceful transfers of power; index movement can miss local organizing and informal protections.

denominator.unit: countries assessed for political rights and civil liberties, plus 13 territories

free_population_share.unit: percent of the world's population living in Free countries

observations.method: Freedom House classification from equally weighted political-rights and civil-liberties totals.
observations.uncertainty: Status categories compress multidimensional scores and can hide within-country regional, group, and institutional variation; population shares rely on external population estimates.
observations.subgroup: Populations living under Free, Partly Free, and Not Free country conditions, including minority and opposition groups whose experiences may diverge from national averages.
observations.counterinterpretation: A national status is not a complete description of every institution or person; some Not Free or Partly Free settings contain meaningful civic spaces and reform openings.

observations.period: 2025; drivers and institutional pathways of decline

main_decline_drivers.value: armed conflicts, coups, erosion of democratic institutions, and authoritarian crackdowns are identified as major drivers

heaviest_impact_areas.value: media freedom, personal expression, and due process have suffered especially heavy impacts over the twenty-year decline

partly_free_transition.value: 19 countries that were Partly Free in 2005 declined to Not Free by 2025, while 9 improved to Free

observations.method: Freedom House longitudinal comparison of country scores, status transitions, and indicator-level narratives.
observations.uncertainty: Driver categories overlap and are not experimental causes; status transitions summarize country-level classification rather than institutional sequences or individual harms.
observations.subgroup: Countries with coups, armed conflict, authoritarian repression, democratic-institutional erosion, media restrictions, or due-process failures.
observations.counterinterpretation: Institutional decline can be interrupted by elections, judicial independence, civil resistance, or reform coalitions; causal pathways differ across regions and regimes.

denominator.unit: countries rated Free in 2005 used for the twenty-year resilience comparison

free_status_persistence.unit: countries, more than 85 percent of the 2005 Free group, that remained Free through 2025

partly_to_free_upgrades.unit: countries upgraded from Partly Free to Free in 2025

upgrade_mechanisms.value: competitive elections, judicial independence, and stronger rule of law contributed to the highlighted upgrades

observations.method: Freedom House longitudinal status comparison and country-level narrative assessment.
observations.uncertainty: The persistence and upgrade comparisons describe status outcomes, not causal effect sizes; selected country narratives may not represent all reform pathways.
observations.subgroup: Democratic systems, reforming countries, electoral institutions, judiciaries, civil society, and populations benefiting from improved rights protections.
observations.counterinterpretation: Resilience is not permanence, and formal status upgrades can coexist with unresolved inequality, exclusion, or localized rights violations.

related_sources.claim: International IDEA provides a complementary democracy-performance and conflict lens.
Freedom House methodology documents the indicator and classification framework.

boundary: This record adds an independent political-rights and civil-liberties route linking freedom decline, conflict, coups, institutional erosion, media and expression, due process, and reform resilience. It uses an expert-coded country and territory index, not respondent-level political attitudes, individual rights histories, causal repression estimates, or a replacement for the International IDEA assessment.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official Freedom House Freedom in the World 2026 PDF and methodology summary were reviewed for the 208-country-and-territory frame, 2025 score changes, status distribution, longitudinal drivers, and resilience findings.
